fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Reading the Sky as a Text", "body": "Chance defines astrotheology not as seminary theology but as the question of how we got the stories behind our religions and mythologies: the story in the stars. His key flip is direction, since myths were not placed in the sky to honor them, the sky was brought down and made into story. He reads Samson, shorn of his hair, as the weakening winter sun, noting Shamash means sun in Babylonian, and sets paronomasia, divinely inspired wordplay on star names, against the pareidolia label materialists pin on the ancients, using Cetus as proof: Menkar, Mira and Deneb Kaitos, also called Diphda, the second frog after Fomalhaut."}, {"title": "Mother Goose Among the Stars", "body": "Drawing on Mary Stewart Adams and The Star Tales of Mother Goose, Chance calls nursery rhymes the training wheels of astrotheology. Meg reads Goosey Goosey Gander, and he maps it onto Cygnus the goose, Cassiopeia as my lady whose shape doubles as stairs, and Cepheus tumbling backward as the old man who wouldn't say his prayers. In Hey Diddle Diddle, Meg spots Leo or Lyra as the cat and fiddle, while Chance reads the cow over the moon as a new moon in Taurus, dates the scene to April and early May, and hears Canis Minor and Canis Major in a 1700s note about the little dog."}, {"title": "Following the Swan From Hamsa to the Norns", "body": "Asking whether Mother Goose is Cygnus, Chance follows the swan through the Paramahamsas, the supreme swans of the Upanishads, and notes that the Hamsa hand is also called the hand of Fatima, Miriam or Mary. He reads Apollo's Hyperborean temple, circled by singing swans, as Cygnus wheeling circumpolar around the extreme north. Then come Perchta, the goose-footed goddess of spinning, the swan maidens of the Volundarkvida including Svanhvit, the fate-weaving Norns and Greek Moirai, and finally Mother Goose herself spinning a yarn. Meg adds her respect for Rudolf Steiner, who claimed high initiates were called swans."}, {"title": "The Tetramorph, Royal Stars and Tarot", "body": "Chance calls the tetramorph the beat that pretty much proves astrotheology in Christianity, and Meg instantly names its man, lion, bull and eagle as the fixed signs. He traces the figures from Ezekiel's creatures, like burning coals and lamps, to the throne of Revelation, where Meg reads the seven lamps of fire as planets. He then pairs the four evangelists with the royal stars: Matthew with Fomalhaut, Mark with Regulus, Luke with Aldebaran, and John, one of the Boanerges or sons of thunder, with Antares. Seeing the same four on the Wheel of Fortune and World cards, he argues tarot is not anti-Christian."}, {"title": "Why Astrotheology Need Not Threaten Faith", "body": "Chance quotes the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America on canon 36 of Laodicea and argues the church attacks a straw man, the idea that astrology means the stars control our lives. He contends initiates have always written esoterically, citing Synesius of Cyrene speaking in fables and Erasmus saying a good man must sometimes conceal the truth. His goal, he says, is to make faith bigger, not undermine it, and he closes on three principles: free will, the truth always being in the room, and as above, so below, echoed in the Lord's Prayer, making the stars messengers of God's will rather than rulers."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: What connects Christianity, Tarot, and the stars? In Astrotheology 101, Chance Garton joins Meg Moonbeam to explore the celestial symbolism woven through biblical stories, sacred art, and even familiar nursery rhymes. Why do a man, an eagle, a bull, and a lion appear around Christ, represent the four evangelists, and occupy the corners of the World and Wheel of Fortune tarot cards? What connects these figures to the fixed signs of the zodiac, and what changes when we begin reading the sky as a language?
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: This illustrated InnerVerse and Meg Moonbeam swapcast introduces astrotheology through recognizable examples, from Mother Goose and Cygnus the swan to the tetramorph and the four Royal Stars, then follows the connections into mythology, astrology, and Christian symbolism. Chance presents his interpretation of how constellations, seasonal patterns, star names, and wordplay became ingredients in stories passed down through generations, and why exploring that celestial language need not undermine Christian faith.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Sun Hidden in the Word Lord", "body": "Chance Garton opens the members' hour by reading Jesus through solar language, from the \"light of the world\" in John 9:5 and the transfigured face that \"did shine as the sun\" in Matthew 17:2 to the countenance in Revelation 1:16 shining like the sun in his strength. He then follows the word Lord: Greek kurios, which Plutarch tied to Kouros, the Persian name for the sun, and Hebrew Adonai, which Chance hears echoing Adonis, the dying and rising Phoenician sun god. Cor means heart, he adds, and the flaming Sacred Heart points straight to Leo, the heart sign ruled by the Sun."}, {"title": "Three Birthdays for the Sun", "body": "Because the Bible never dates the nativity, Chance lays out three solar candidates for it. At the spring equinox the sun enters Aries, and Jesus as the Lamb, whose cleansing blood belongs to Mars, the ruler of Aries, fits a year being reborn. At the autumnal equinox, when some ancient calendars began the year, the sun leaves Virgo, so a savior is literally born of the virgin. At the winter solstice the sun seems to stand still for three days before climbing north again, rising with Virgo on December 25th, which Chance reads as both the birth and the three days in the tomb."}, {"title": "December 25th Was Never Christianity's Alone", "body": "Chance gathers solstice lore from far beyond the church: Amaterasu hiding in her cave, the beam of light entering Newgrange, Hopi kiva prayers for the sun's return, Ovid's Janus calling midwinter the start of the new sun, Plutarch's Isis giving birth to Harpocrates, the Calendar of Antiochus marking December 25th as the birthday of the sun, and Macrobius describing Dionysus as an infant at the solstice. When Pope Leo I and Augustine insisted Christmas had nothing to do with the sun, he argues, they proved people believed it did. Meg Moonbeam calls the demonizing of astrology an inversion the Age of Pisces is finally shedding."}, {"title": "Mary, Virgo and the Sign of Isaiah", "body": "Chance argues that calling Mary a virgin amounts to calling her Virgo, since parthenos, the Greek word for her virginity, is the very name of the constellation. He rereads Isaiah 7:14 through the Hebrew, where the word for sign, ot, is the same one Genesis 1:14 uses for the heavenly lights serving as signs and seasons, and the virgin is simply a maiden. Invoking the Italian pun traduttore, traditore, he warns that translation betrays, then offers Emmanuel as Om Nu El, our God Om, while insisting astrotheology is no substitution cipher but layered poetry."}, {"title": "Miriam, the Sea and the Mothers of Saviors", "body": "Chance traces Mary back to Miriam, the sister of Moses, whose name means sea and who is only named once the Hebrews reach the Red Sea. Her song of the horse and rider thrown into the sea, he says, matches Sagittarius setting as Gemini, the children of Israel, rises in the east. Moses' adopted mother, called Thermuthis by Josephus and Meres by Latin church writers, joins Mary, Maia and Myrrha among the mothers of saviors. Miriam turns white as snow like Venus, Mary becomes Queen of Heaven and Stella Maris, and when Miriam dies at Kadesh the water runs out."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "The sun is at its weakest as it starts to climb back up from the winter solstice, so it's like a baby.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "What is more of the representation or the literal savior of our world than the sun? There would be nothing here without the sun.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It's just, as you're sharing, wild the inversion that has taken place when it comes to Christianity, the Bible, the meanings of things, how astrology has been demonized.", "author": "Meg Moonbeam", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/d35af703-c3c3-4169-bff5-e62be8067732/MEG-MOONBEAM.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It can be hard to hear for some of us, but this is us coming out of the Age of Pisces and really dispelling these illusions that need to be dispelled.", "author": "Meg Moonbeam", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/d35af703-c3c3-4169-bff5-e62be8067732/MEG-MOONBEAM.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The translator is a traitor because you just cannot really ever one-to-one translate from one language to another.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "What feels more likely when you just run it through your life experience? That a human woman gets pregnant and gives birth, or that a celestial virgin gives birth to the sun?", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Astrotheology is not a jigsaw puzzle where everything fits in one place with only one right answer. It's more poetry than that.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Jesus and Moses are so similar that I think the Old Testament and New Testament were written at about the same time.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It kind of makes sense if Christ is the King of Kings, why not let Mary be the Queen of Queens?", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It's sad, actually, because we could be using the Bible and astrology and tarot together, like you were saying, but people get stuck in the certain beliefs of the different aspects of it.", "author": "Meg Moonbeam", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/d35af703-c3c3-4169-bff5-e62be8067732/MEG-MOONBEAM.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "It turns out they are literally like the way that you would pull up a document in Spanish and translate it to English.
